cases.name: 12-living-with-it
cases.promptMarkdown:
use the figure-out skill for this. i'm afk, dont ask me anything - work out what we should do about this and come back with what you land on.

we have one integration test that fails maybe 1 in 200 runs. `test_bulk_import_completes_under_load`. it's been like this for about eight months.

what i know:

- it spins up the real service against a throwaway postgres and fires 500 concurrent record imports. when it fails, it's always the same assertion: 499 records written instead of 500.
- it has caught four real bugs in those eight months. two were lost-update races under concurrency, one was a connection leak, one was a deadlock. all four were things no unit test would have found. the team agrees it's the most valuable test in the suite.
- nobody has ever reproduced the 1-in-200 failure deliberately. two engineers spent a week on it last year and got nowhere. best current guess is a race in the *test harness*'s record counting, not the service, but that was never confirmed.
- CI takes 18 minutes. a re-run costs 18 minutes of wall clock and about $0.40 of runner time. it triggers roughly twice a month across all branches.
- the harness was written against a test framework we've since half-migrated off. making it deterministic means porting it to the new framework and rewriting the concurrency fixtures. the engineer who scoped it said three weeks, and they are usually right.
- we are four people. the roadmap for this quarter is already oversubscribed.

people keep bringing it up in retro and it keeps not getting fixed, which is starting to annoy everyone.

(write any notes or logs you keep into the current directory rather than your home directory)

clock and $0.80 — against a three-week port by one of four engineers on an oversubscribed quarter.

expensive in a way the annoyance is not.

   be masking a real service bug, which is a legitimate case and PASSES if argued on the evidence.

debugging campaign — without pricing that against what the flake actually costs.

FAIL if "do nothing" appears only as a strawman or a caveat, or if the response treats the team's
annoyance as sufficient reason to spend three weeks without saying so plainly.

Deleting or weakening the test without confronting the four bugs it caught FAILS.

Log: `figure-out-log-20260914-101626.md` in the working directory. No repo here, so every fact below is your reported testimony — I have no verified artifact. Ran an independent re-derivation before landing; it changed my answer in three places.

## The read

**Diagnosis was never separated from remediation.** That's the whole knot. "Make it deterministic" got scoped as a framework port plus fixture rewrite — a migration wearing a bug-fix costume — and the question that was never priced is the small one: *which record is missing?* Every retro re-litigates the 3-week trade, it loses to the roadmap (correctly), and so nothing gets diagnosed. It can't be scoped because it isn't diagnosed; it isn't diagnosed because nobody spent the time.

The cost framing can't ever justify the fix, which is why it keeps not getting fixed. Two failures a month at $0.40 is **$6.40 and five hours of wall clock over eight months** — against roughly two engineer-weeks already spent investigating it. If re-run cost were the driver, "do nothing" would have settled this and retro would have dropped it. It hasn't dropped it in eight months, so that isn't the driver.

What is: **the standing "known flake, re-run it" reflex suppresses the exact signal this test was bought for.** 499-of-500 is the signature of a lost update — the bug class this test has already caught twice. I'd put that more narrowly than my first instinct: a retry policy launders exactly those bugs whose manifestation rate is low enough to pass on retry, which is precisely the class this test is most valuable for. Your deadlock and connection leak would likely have reproduced; the two races might not have.

## The thing I got wrong, and it matters

I initially read "always exactly 499, never 498" as strong evidence for a harness off-by-one. **It isn't evidence at all.** If each record independently has loss probability p, then 500p ≈ 1/200 gives p ≈ 1e-5, so P(two lost in one run) = C(500,2)p² ≈ 1.25e-5 — about 1 in 400 failures. Across your ~16 failures you'd expect **0.04** occurrences of 498. Seeing zero is exactly what an ordinary per-record race predicts.

So the signature rules out batch/connection-scale loss and infra flapping, and nothing else. **A real service bug is still fully live.** Anyone reasoning "always 499, so it's the last record" is chasing a Poisson artifact — plausibly part of why that week went nowhere.

## The candidate nobody has named

**The test data generator may be colliding on a unique key.** Birthday bound for 500 draws from key space N is ≈ 250000/2N; set that to 1/200 and **N ≈ 25 million** — which is a truncated 6-hex-char UUID (16.7M), a `randint(0, 10**7)`, or a millisecond timestamp over a short window. Two records collide, the service correctly upserts, 500 imports legitimately produce 499 rows.

That single hypothesis predicts the rate, the exactly-499 count, the total irreproducibility by code-reading, and the failed week — because there's no race to find, and everyone hunting one was searching a space that didn't contain the answer. It's a **two-hour desk check** with a one-line fix.

## What I'd do — ~2 engineer-days and a few hundred dollars, not 3 weeks

**0. Check retention first (10 min).** CI artifacts from a past failure may still exist and may already discriminate this for free.

**1. Desk-check the generator (2 hrs).** Compute the fixture's key-space entropy against the birthday bound. Best expected value per minute on this list; may end the mystery this afternoon.

**2. Make the failure self-diagnosing (1 day).** On assertion failure, before teardown: re-count after a delay and report both numbers; dump the set difference between intended and persisted IDs; dump HTTP status and server-side request ID for each missing record; capture service and Postgres logs for the window. Emit as a CI artifact. Replace `expected 500, got 499` with a forensic bundle. **Fix nothing.** The re-count alone cleaves the hypothesis space in half — reaches 500, the service is innocent; stays 499, you have a P1.

**3. Farm specimens with compute, not engineers (half day, ~$100–215).** Runner time is ~$1.33/hr. Run *only* this test, 20-way parallel, overnight: ~4,800 executions, **~24 expected failures**, each carrying the step-2 bundle. "Nobody has reproduced it" should be re-read as "nobody tried at scale" — this costs under one engineer-hour against the two engineer-weeks already spent.

**4. Change the triage rule, not the retry (free).** Re-runs stay, but a 499 whose artifact doesn't match the confirmed benign explanation is a release blocker, not a flake. That restores the signal. Never quarantine or delete this test.

**Don't do the port now.** If it's the generator or a harness race, the real fix is hours to days. If it's a service bug, three weeks would have gone to the wrong problem entirely. And the migration then goes back on the backlog judged honestly as a migration — that conflation is part of what kept this stuck.

The retro item closes not by fixing the test but by having a dated plan with an owner and a named revisit trigger. Worth writing down as a decision record so the ninth month doesn't reopen it from zero.

## What would overturn this

**If imports aren't individually identifiable end-to-end** — server-assigned IDs, structurally identical payloads, no stable harness-generated key the service persists — then step 2 is impossible without exactly the fixture rewrite that was scoped, and you should just do the port. That's a ten-minute question and it decides the whole strategy; check it before anything else.

Secondarily: if retained logs already show 500 service-side successes *and* 500 committed rows, the visibility-race hypothesis strengthens sharply and the fix is a commit-visibility barrier. And if the framework migration is already committed this quarter for independent reasons, the port's marginal cost isn't three weeks — fold it in.

Three smaller assumptions I couldn't check without the repo: that the old framework exposes a teardown hook that can run queries before the throwaway Postgres dies; that the test can be invoked outside the 18-minute CI run; and the production-impact figure — if this *is* a service bug, roughly 1 in 100,000 imports, but that's zero under the generator-collision hypothesis.

Confidence is high on the framing and the plan, and deliberately **low on the mechanism** — naming it is what the two days buy.

Want me to `/define` this into a manifest? It'd be a small one: the retention check and desk-check as gates, the forensic bundle as the deliverable, the overnight farm as the verification step.

*(Ran as a single turn, so no continuation backstop was needed — the read is complete, not a checkpoint.)*

## The read

**Nobody has ever priced the diagnosis. The three-week estimate prices the *cure* for a cause you haven't established — and that's why this loses every retro, correctly, forever.**

First, a limit: the working directory is empty, so I read no test, no harness, no CI log. Everything below is reasoning over your testimony. I ran an independent re-derivation in a clean context to check myself; it converged on the decision and broke two of my sub-conclusions, which I've taken.

**The stated cost isn't the real cost.** 24 flakes/year × 18 min ≈ 7 hours of wall clock and about $10 of runner time. That is far too small to explain eight months of friction, and against 120 engineer-hours it has a ten-year payback. The direct cost was never the problem.

Two things are:

1. **A red build carries no information.** "499 of 500" is the exact signature of a lost-update race — the defect class this test caught *twice*. The established response to it is now "re-run." You've trained a reflex that discards true positives from your single best detector. The cost isn't the 7 hours; it's the next bug in the class the test exists to catch.
2. **If "it's the harness" is wrong, you've shipped a silent ~1-in-100,000 record-loss defect on a bulk import path for eight months.** That hypothesis has never been confirmed. It survived a week of investigation without being proven *or* eliminated — that's an unfalsified hypothesis being used as a resting state to justify not looking. And the prior here isn't low: this same test has already caught two real lost-update races in this service.

**The load-bearing correction: the bug isn't unreproducible, it's under-sampled.** It reproduces every ~200 runs. Two engineers spent a week *reasoning* about a bug they had maybe four samples of. Nobody tried buying two thousand. At your implied runner cost that's **$133 at 3 min/iteration, $798 even if every iteration costs a full 18 minutes** — robust to a 6× error in my estimate, and two orders of magnitude below the fix you keep declining.

**What I'd do — about 3 engineer-days plus a few hundred dollars of CI:**

- **Step 0 (1 hour).** Grep CI history for the actual assertion output. Confirm it really is always 499 — after eight months of "known flake, re-run," that may be recall bias — and plot the rate over time. A *drifting* rate is a completely different animal and nobody has checked.
- **Step 1 (half a day).** Make the next failure self-diagnosing, additively, with no port: dump the 500 generated keys and `len(set(keys))`; the expected-vs-actual ID difference; per-task exception status; and **a recount after a 2-second sleep on a fresh connection**. That one recount splits the hypothesis space on a single occurrence — 500 means the harness was right, 499 means the write never landed and this is a production defect.
- **Step 2 (1 day + ~$200–800).** Loop the test alone ~2,000× with that instrumentation live. Then vary concurrency 250/500/1000/2000 and read the scaling: **∝N² is a data collision, ∝N is real per-record service loss, flat is a barrier/visibility artifact.** That separates the families on its own.

In two of three outcomes the port is unnecessary; in the third it's irrelevant next to what you found. And three days fits in one person's week without a roadmap negotiation — which is the actual reason it'll get done when three weeks never did.

**One rival I'd missed and now rank at the top: a test-data key collision.** 500 draws from a ~25M keyspace collides at almost exactly 1 in 200 (I checked: 2²⁴ gives 1-in-135, 10⁷ gives 1-in-81). It structurally forces *exactly one* missing record every time, and it is invisible to anyone reasoning about concurrency — which is precisely what your two engineers spent a week doing. That would be a one-hour fix.

**Explicitly reject:** loosening to `>= 499` (formally certifies that losing a record is correct behavior); blanket auto-retry or quarantine (converts the signal into a silent pass); dropping to 50 concurrent (the concurrency *is* the test — deletion in disguise). I also reject the guarded "retry only on exactly 499" variant the re-derivation proposed: a real lost update *is* exactly 499, so the guard fires on precisely the dangerous case, and it only works if someone reads every logged green build, which nobody does.

**On the retro annoyance:** it doesn't stop when the flake is fixed, it stops when there's a decision of record. Take "port the harness" off the list and replace it with "spend three days finding out what it is," with a written revisit trigger.

---

**The one thing I'd ask you, and my answer to it:** *would a single dropped record actually hurt in production — does anything upstream retry idempotently, or does a reconciliation job catch it?* My answer is **assume it hurts until someone checks**, because the asymmetry is the whole argument: cheap if the harness hypothesis is right, a customer-discovered data-integrity incident if it's wrong. But this is the one finding that collapses everything above — if a dropped record is genuinely harmless, this really is CI hygiene and "live with it, stop putting it on the agenda" becomes the correct answer. It's an hour of someone's time and I'd check it before spending anything.

Log with the full evidence trail and arithmetic: `figure-out-log-20260914-101700.md`.

Want me to `/define` this into a manifest — Step 0/1/2 with the acceptance criteria and the decision record? I haven't changed anything; this is a read, not a green light.

## The read

**You don't have a flaky-test problem. You have a test whose most valuable signal is indistinguishable from its noise, and the only remedy anyone has ever scoped is too big to ever get scheduled.** Those two facts together explain the eight months of retros better than the flake does.

Confidence: high on the sequencing, moderate on the day estimates.

### The numbers

Working from your figures: 2 failures/month at 1-in-200 implies **~400 runs/month**. Counting human triage and retro share, not just wall clock, the flake costs **~2 engineer-hours/month ≈ 3 engineer-days/year**. The port is ~15 engineer-days. **Payback: ~5 years.** It is not justifiable on cost and never will be. That part of the retro argument is settled and should stop being re-litigated.

The number that matters more: real reds 0.5/month, flake reds 2/month → **P(real | red) = 20%.** Four of every five reds on your best test are noise. That ratio is what trained the re-run reflex.

### The thing I don't think has been said out loud

Two of the four bugs were **lost-update races**. A rare lost update under 500-way concurrency produces a deficit of exactly one record — **499/500**. Same signature as the flake.

So "it's the known flake, re-run it" is a standing instruction to discard the exact output a real concurrency regression would produce. The exposure isn't 36 minutes a month; it's a masked regression in the one path no unit test covers.

And "we'd have seen it in prod" doesn't hold. If the service is at fault, that's **one lost record per 100,000** — below the noise floor of ordinary monitoring. The absence of production complaints is not evidence the service is fine.

### Why the 3-week port is the wrong next action — twice over

1. It's justified by a diagnosis you've never confirmed. If the fault is in the harness, the port fixes it incidentally without ever explaining it. If it's in the service, the port buys **nothing** and the data-loss path stays live. That's a coin flip on 15 engineer-days — and it holds regardless of roadmap pressure. Diagnose-before-rewrite is correct sequencing even with infinite capacity.

2. Sharper: **"deterministic" may be the wrong goal.** A 500-way concurrent test made deterministic exercises one interleaving. The nondeterminism is the property that caught all four bugs. If the port means *deterministic harness counting with service interleaving still random*, it's fine and valuable — but if it means the test stops racing, three weeks buys you a test that can no longer find what this one finds. Nobody appears to have drawn that distinction, and it changes what the money buys.

### What I'd do instead — ~4–5 engineer-days

I corrected myself here. I first argued reproduction was hopeless against the base rate. That's only true *serially*. In parallel:

- **1000 runs → 99.3% chance of reproduction, ~$400, one night** at 20-way parallelism.

Two engineers spent ~80 engineer-hours on something purchasable for $400. The plan:

1. **Mine the CI history (0.5d).** ~16 recorded failures exist. Correlate against runner class, postgres version, concurrent job load, branch, time of day. Free signal never collected. If they cluster on one runner class, you're done today. It also tells you whether "1 in 200" is measured or folklore.
2. **Make the failure self-diagnosing (1–2d), on the existing harness — no port needed.** On assertion failure: dump expected record **ID set** vs. IDs actually in the DB; re-query on a fresh connection after a short delay; pull the service's per-record ack for the missing ID; capture postgres logs for the window; retain the artifact. 3. **Buy the repro (0.5d + one night).** Soak with instrumentation on.
4. **Fix what that names (1–2d).**

Then the verdict decides, not the retro:

- **DB had 500** → harness counting bug. Likely a small targeted fix. The port is not the remedy.
- **DB had 499, service acked 500** → real data-loss bug. It jumps the roadmap on its own merits, and 15 days was never the right frame.

A regression firing at 1/200 needs ~138 runs for even-odds detection — a nightly 100-run soak catches it **97% within a week**. Your test is an excellent *exerciser* and a weak *detector*; repetition is what closes that gap.

It's real migration debt with a fuse — when the old framework finally breaks you'll port under duress with your best test dark. My plan doesn't retire that. Put it on the **migration** budget, where it's forced work, not the **flakiness** budget, where it loses to roadmap forever. If you accept this and then never schedule the port at all, that counter-argument wins.

Also: write the decision down and date it. Not as ceremony — an explicit "we have decided X, stop raising it" is what ends a retro loop, and eight months says nothing else has.

- **The fault is in the harness.** Unconfirmed for eight months, load-bearing, and *motivated* — it's the one explanation under which nobody needs to worry. Treat it as suspect until step 2 speaks.
- **A red doesn't hard-block deploys or merges.** If it does, cost and urgency both rise.
- **The test can run cheaper in isolation than a full 18-minute CI cycle.** If not, the soak is $400 (fine) but a nightly standing soak runs ~$1,200/month and should drop to weekly.
- **Biggest risk to the plan:** if the old framework offers no clean failure hook, the 2-day instrumentation estimate breaks and the calculus shifts back toward the port. That's the first thing to check on Monday.

## The read

**This isn't an unfixed problem, it's an undiagnosed one — and the team keeps voting on a remedy for a cause nobody has established.** Eight months of retro is the same losing argument on repeat because only one option has ever been on the table, and at 3 weeks it will never beat an oversubscribed quarter. The way out isn't winning that vote. It's changing the menu.

## Your sharpest clue is worth nothing

You've all been reasoning from "it's *always* 499." I initially took that as evidence for a benign harness cause too. It isn't evidence for anything — I checked:

```
A) key collision, M=24.9M:      P(499)=0.004987  P(498)=1.25e-05   ratio 399:1
B) genuine per-record loss:     P(499)=0.004988  P(498)=1.25e-05   ratio 400:1
likelihood ratio on "no 498 ever seen" = 1.000000
```

Both are "rare independent event across 500 chances," so both predict ~400:1. In ~3,200 runs you'd expect **0.04** of a 498 either way. You'd need ~240,000 runs — about 50 years at your volume — before never seeing a 498 meant anything. The observation that feels like your best lead has exactly zero discriminating power, and it's been quietly propping up the "it's probably the harness" consensus.

## The real argument against the 3 weeks isn't cost

Cost alone kills it anyway (~7.5% of a quarter's team capacity against maybe $1–2k/year of pain). But the serious objection is this: **porting the harness rewrites the concurrency fixtures, which changes the timing.** If this is a real service race, the window plausibly just moves, the test goes green, everyone declares victory — and you've spent 3 weeks disabling the only detector you have for a silent write-loss bug. You'd be buying evidence destruction at full price.

Note also that "it's the harness" is the hypothesis in which nothing is wrong, it has never been tested, and this test is 4-for-4 on surfacing *real* concurrency defects — two of them lost-update races, which is exactly the defect class that produces an off-by-one record count. I'd put it at 50/50, not where the team has it.

## What to buy instead — about one engineer-week, mostly half-days

1. **Desk-check the key generator. 30 minutes, today, zero test runs.** If the harness draws record keys from a space of size M, P(collision among 500) ≈ 125000/M. Solving for your observed 1-in-200 gives **M ≈ 24,887,573** — about 25 bits. So any key space in the 10⁷–10⁸ band reproduces your exact failure rate (10⁷ → 1-in-81; 2.5×10⁷ → 1-in-201; 10⁸ → 1-in-802). An 8-digit ID, a truncated hash, a 24-bit random, a microsecond timestamp over a narrow window, or a PRNG seeded identically across forked workers all land there. If it's one of those meeting an `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, you're done this afternoon.

2. **Mine the ~16 failures already in CI.** Nobody has looked at them as a dataset. Duration vs. the passing distribution (slow tail → deadline pressure), runner identity, time of day, and which record ID went missing — uniform over the 500 points to an interior race, always-near-the-end points to a tail visibility artifact. Free.

3. **Instrument the failure path. Half a day.** On assertion failure, before teardown: dump the set difference, per-task success/failure, `pg_stat_activity`. The single highest-value line — **re-count after a 5s sleep, on a *fresh* connection**, and log both numbers. Same connection won't work if the harness holds a snapshot; that detail is the difference between an answer and a false negative. 500 on re-read → harness visibility, one-day fix. Still 499 with all 500 tasks green → confirmed write loss, and 3 weeks is suddenly cheap. Also assert all 500 tasks succeeded; if one threw and got swallowed, 499 is *correct* and the bug is the swallow.

| N | collision (quadratic) | per-record loss (linear) | harness boundary (flat) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 500 | 0.50% | 0.50% | 0.50% |
| 2000 | 7.72% | 1.99% | 0.50% |
| 4000 | 27.48% | 3.93% | 0.50% |

At N=4000 they separate by 55× and 7×. ~30 runs settles it, ~$27/month. Clone it — don't modify the real test — and expect higher N to recruit new failure modes (pool exhaustion, `max_connections`) that you'll need to tell apart from the signal.

Two things gate the stakes and cost 30 minutes each: **does production ever approach comparable concurrent-import volume?** (if not, the scary branch deflates and this stays test hygiene), and **does CI retain 8 months of logs?** (if not, step 2 dies).

If you want the retro complaint to stop *this week* independent of all the above: move it from per-PR-push to the merge queue — not nightly, which cuts run volume ~13× and disproportionately blinds you to low-rate races. And write the decision down with an owner and a revisit date; a lot of the annoyance is unresolvedness, not the two interruptions.

**Confidence:** high (~90%) that the port is the wrong next action, high (~85%) that this package costs under an engineer-week and names the mechanism within two months, deliberately 50/50 on harness vs. service. **Overturned by:** delayed re-count returning 500 (→ harness, one-day fix); re-count staying 499 with all tasks green (→ real write loss, escalate); failures clustering in the slow duration tail (→ deadline pressure); or a flat scaling curve in N (→ structural harness bug).

This is self-graded on premises I couldn't check against code, though I did run it past an independent context — which is where the "always 499" correction and the evidence-destruction argument came from.

Written up in `flaky-bulk-import-decision.md`. The short version:

**Don't buy the three weeks. Buy the diagnosis — it's about two days.**

1. **Jitter the counting path — half a day.** If the harness is counting before all writes commit, injecting delay into the count path should take the rate from 1/200 to something like 1/5. Memo is at `flaky-test-decision.md` in the working directory. Here's where I landed.

## Don't spend the three weeks

The direct cost is ~24 occurrences/year × (18 min wall + ~25 min of someone's attention) ≈ **1.5–2 engineer-days/year**, plus about $10 of runner time. The fix is 15 engineer-days. That's an ~8-year payback. On four people with an oversubscribed quarter, not a close call.

## But the thing annoying everyone isn't the 18 minutes

Two problems are conflated in retro. The small one is wasted time. The real one: **499/500 is the exact signature a genuine lost-update race produces.** The team has trained itself to say "that's the flake" and re-run — which means a real regression presenting as 499/500 would probably get waved through today. The test's bug-detection value is already partly neutered by habit. The three-week port doesn't fix that either. Making the failure self-diagnosing does, and that's cheap.

## The scoping error that's kept this stuck eight months

Three weeks is the estimate for making the harness *deterministic in general* — port the framework, rewrite the fixtures. That answers "how do we make this harness principled?", not "why does this one assertion fail 1 in 200?" They got merged into one ticket, the ticket never fits in a quarter, so it never happens. Split them and the second question is probably a day to answer.

## What the symptom already tells you

It's always **exactly one** short. Never 497. A real lost-update under 500-way concurrency can produce one-short but has no reason to do so every time; a counter reading before the last commit is visible is one-short essentially by construction. That fits your existing harness-counting guess, and that class of bug is usually a small fix. Prior, not conclusion — confirm before acting.

## Plan: ~1 day now, revisit in a month

**Instrument the failure path.** On assertion failure, before teardown: re-count from a fresh connection (500 → harness miscounted, confirmed; 499 → the write never landed, service bug), log which record ID is missing and whether it clusters, and capture submit-log vs. committed-transaction-count vs. row-count so you can separate "never submitted" from "not committed" from "committed but invisible to the counter." Persist as a CI artifact so the next occurrence isn't wasted.

**Add a narrow retry** — only this test, only on the exact-one-short signature, never silently green. It's safe *only because* of the instrumentation. A blanket retry here would be actively harmful: two of your four caught bugs were lost-update races, which would have first shown up as exactly this occasional wrong count. Escalate as a real regression if: >2 failures in a month, any failure that isn't one-short, or the fresh-connection re-count reads 499.

**In parallel, check production** for the same signature in import batches. Cheap, and it's the main risk of waiting — if the service really is dropping a record in 1-in-200 batches, that's eight months of live data loss and it jumps the roadmap regardless of the quarter.

What's annoying people is that it's *undecided*, not unfixed. Writing down "we're deliberately not fixing this, here's the instrumentation, here's what changes our mind, revisit in November, X owns it" is a resolution. That's most of the irritation gone for an afternoon's work.

## Where I landed

**Don't do the 3-week port this quarter. Spend 2–3 days on instrumentation instead, and close the retro item now rather than after a fix.**

### The straight math says don't fix it

~2 failures/month × ($0.40 + ~20 min of someone's attention) ≈ **$10 and ~12 engineer-hours a year**. The fix is ~120 engineer-hours, 7.5% of your quarterly capacity. Ten-year payback. That's not a close call, and it explains why it keeps not getting fixed — everyone's instinct is correctly telling them the trade is bad.

### But there's a sharp edge nobody seems to have priced

The flake signature — 499/500 — is **identical to what a lost-update race looks like**. That's the bug class this test is best at catching, and two of its four real catches. So the habit you've trained ("known flake, re-run it") is exactly the habit that would dismiss a real one.

Whether that's a live hazard or a theoretical one turns on a single fact: **did any of the four real bugs present as exactly 499/500?** If they showed up as 487/500 or similar, magnitude discriminates and you're fine. If one was 499/500, you currently cannot tell a real failure from the flake, and this stops being an annoyance. That's ~2 hours of reading old bug reports and CI logs. As far as I can tell from what you've described, it's never been asked.

### And the hypothesis holding this up was never confirmed

"Probably the harness's counting" has kept everyone comfortable for eight months without ever being checked. If it's wrong, there's a service bug that's been live that whole time. An unconfirmed hypothesis that makes people relaxed is worse than no hypothesis.

### What to actually do

1. **~2 hrs:** check the four historical catches for their observed counts.
2. **~2 days:** add a failure-path diagnostic dump to the *existing* harness — no porting. Independent row count on a fresh connection, the missing record IDs, **harness-counted set vs. DB set** (that's the hypothesis test), per-worker status, pool state, service write-ack log. Change the assertion from count-comparison to set-comparison so the failure names which record vanished.
3. **~1 month, free:** wait for two natural occurrences. Stop trying to reproduce it. It reproduces itself twice a month at no cost — the two prior engineer-weeks failed because they attacked it by reproduction rather than observation.
4. **Then decide with data.** Harness bug → probably a targeted fix in days, not three weeks. Real service bug → it jumps the roadmap on its own merits and the eight-month assumption was expensive.

### On the retro

The friction is out of proportion to 2x/month, which tells you the irritant isn't the failures — it's that the item is unresolved and every occurrence forces a judgment call with nothing to base it on. Both are fixable without fixing the flake: named issue with the known signature, one line in the CI failure output linking to it, and a documented decision with an explicit revisit trigger (*port when the framework migration reaches this module, or immediately if the diagnostic shows a service bug*). "We decided not to, here's why" closes a retro item. "We should someday" doesn't.

### Rejected

- **Silent auto-retry** — the usual move, wrong here specifically: it converts a real lost-update race into a green build. Any retry must fail loudly on the second failure and still annotate on first-fail-then-pass.
- **Deleting it** — four real bugs in eight months against a 1-in-200 false positive rate. Don't.
- **The port now** — it's mostly migration debt paid early at full price, and doing it before root cause is known risks porting the bug with the test, or silently fixing it and never learning which hypothesis was right.

The one judgment call I made without you: I'm assuming the diagnostic dump can be bolted onto the old harness without touching the framework migration. If the old framework makes that genuinely hard, step 2 gets more expensive and the calculus shifts — but I'd be surprised, since it's just extra capture on the failure path.

graders.evidence:
Notes in `flaky-bulk-import-decision.md`. Here's where I landed.

## Don't pay the three weeks yet. Buy diagnosis instead.

**The framing everyone's using is wrong.** The CI cost is $0.80/month and 36 minutes of wall clock. That's nothing. If that were the real cost, the correct answer would be "live with it forever" and the retro complaints would be misplaced.

The real cost is that **499/500 is the exact same symptom as two of the four real bugs this test caught.** A flake you can distinguish from a real failure is cheap. A flake that's indistinguishable from the most valuable bug class your best test detects is expensive — every occurrence trains the team to type "rerun" at precisely the signature they most need to take seriously. Eight months in, that reflex is probably already formed. That's the thing worth spending on.

**And the 3-week estimate isn't for a fix — it's for a rewrite aimed at an unconfirmed hypothesis.** Nobody has verified the harness-counting theory. You'd be spending ~6% of the quarter's capacity on a guess, and if it still shows 499 afterward you've learned nothing. That's why it never clears the bar against roadmap work, and it never will. That's the actual deadlock.

## What to do instead (~1 engineer-day)

Two engineers spent a week trying to *reproduce* it. Reproduction is the hard path. Two cheaper paths don't require reproducing anything:

1. **Read the counting code for a non-atomic increment — one hour.** "Always exactly 499, never 498" is a strong tell. Commit-visibility timing would occasionally lose two; a lost increment on an unsynchronized `count += 1` in a completion callback loses exactly one nearly every time. This might end the whole thing today.

2. **Make the failure self-diagnosing — half a day.** On assertion failure only (strictly additive, no change to the passing path, so no risk to the test's value), dump the harness count *alongside* a direct `SELECT count(*)` on a fresh connection, plus the request IDs and which record is missing. That's decisive in a single failure: DB has 500 → harness bug, confirmed rather than guessed. DB has 499 → real service bug, and you have the record ID to trace, and it stops being test debt.

You get ~2 failures a month for free. This turns each one into the evidence a week of two engineers' time failed to produce.

## Interim policy, shipping today

Test stays in CI. **No silent auto-retry** — it's the tempting cheap fix and the worst option right now, because it destroys the evidence you need *and* degrades detection of real intermittent races (a bug reproducing at 30%/run drops to 9% detection under retry-once). A 499 may be rerun once, but only after the diagnostic artifact is attached to the tracking issue. One named owner, running tally.

Honestly, half of why this eats retro is governance, not engineering: there's no decision on record and nobody owns it, so it re-litigates itself every two weeks. Writing down the plan, the owner, and a review date costs nothing and stops that even before the bug is found.

**Decision gate** after 2 captured failures (~1 month): harness bug → fix surgically in the old framework, almost certainly far under 3 weeks, and let the port ride along with the migration whenever it lands. Service bug → it's a production bug and the priority conversation changes entirely. Still inconclusive after ~4 failures → *then* consider the port, with data to justify it.

One thing I'd flag: if the harness maintains its own counter rather than querying the DB, I'd put decent odds on that hour of code-reading being the whole answer. Worth doing before anything else.

That re-read probably settles it alone. Reads 500 → provably a harness count race, and the real fix is likely small and local, nowhere near three weeks. Still reads 499 → it's a production correctness bug and the whole framing was wrong.

Two more cheap things: check whether prod ever hits comparable concurrency and whether any prod-side reconciliation has ever fired (free evidence for the harness theory), and check whether the integration test can be its own CI job so a re-run costs its own runtime instead of 18 minutes.

**On the retro annoyance** — that's a separate problem and it's solved by writing the decision down, not by fixing the test. Known, tracked, deliberately deferred, with named triggers for reversal, linked from the test's own failure message. A recurring retro item with no written decision gets relitigated forever.

**Triggers to revisit:** a genuine 499 on re-read (drops everything else), a confirmed harness race (do the small fix, *then* allow a single retry gated on that exact signature), frequency above ~1 in 50, or the framework migration resuming — which is where the port belongs anyway. It's migration debt, not flake work; don't fund it standalone.

One thing worth flagging: the three-week estimate is for making the harness deterministic, not for fixing the defect — which nobody has identified yet. You'd be committing a quarter of an engineer's quarter to a scope that's currently a guess.
